summary: Earth Science Autopilot is an automated statistical discovery platform built for NASA Space Apps 2026. Users select any global region and Earth system variable such as temperature, precipitation, or soil moisture to instantly generate multi-year time series and run automated Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope, and t-test significance checks. Unlike passive data viewers, our Autopilot scans variables to rank statistically significant anomalies, removes seasonal noise, and enables side-by-side comparison of regions experiencing opposite climate trends. Deployed live on the web, it transforms raw NASA satellite and model datasets into verifiable, plain-language climate insights in seconds without coding.
details:
Overview

True Earth Trends Detective (The Earth Science Autopilot) is a free web app built for the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge. Usually, checking if a climate trend is real requires downloading huge satellite files and writing complex code. Our app makes this process simple for everyone. Users can type a basic question or click anywhere on our global map to explore 23 environmental variables across 11 Earth systems, turning raw satellite records into clear scientific reports in seconds.

How It Works

Instead of letting AI guess climate numbers, our app relies on real satellite data and proven math. When a user picks a location, the system pulls live data from NASA Common Metadata Repository (CMR) missions like MODIS, GPM, SMAP, and SWOT, along with NOAA weather stations and Open-Meteo historical climate records. Our TypeScript engine removes normal seasonal ups and downs and runs trusted statistical tests, including the Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s slope, linear regression, and Holt-Winters forecasting. This shows whether a change over the decades is truly significant or just normal weather variation.

What Makes Our Approach Creative

Most climate websites only show colorful maps or raw charts, leaving users to guess what the lines actually mean. Our app acts like a smart research guide that explains the math in plain English. It turns complex numbers like p-values and slope rates into simple visual badges and clear takeaways. Users can also compare two places side by side to see opposite trends, check how different Earth systems affect each other, and download their findings as CSV or JSON files.

Benefits and Intended Impact

We built this platform so students, teachers, journalists, and local leaders can study real climate trends without needing advanced coding skills or expensive software. It also saves experienced researchers hours of manual data cleanup. Anyone can use the maps and analysis tools right away as a guest with no login required, or create a free account to save their projects in the cloud.

Tools, Tech Stack, and AI Disclosure

Our live app is hosted at vercel.app (with our full data catalog at vercel.app/resources) and built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Our source code is open to everyone on GitHub under the MIT License, and all climate data comes from NASA Earthdata CMR, NOAA CDO, and Open-Meteo ERA5. To follow NASA Space Apps rules, we also share how we used AI: We used ChatGPT and Antigravity AI (Claude and Gemini) during development to help write interface code, draft text, and route search questions inside the app, while all climate data and statistical math remain 100% real and deterministic with Prediction Graph logics coded into the System.
